articles.title: Hackers Cripple US Election Disclosure System Ahead of Midterms
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox The elections will determine whether US President Donald Trump’s Republicans maintain their majorities in Congress for the next two years. PHOTO: REUTERS Published Oct 28, 2026, 09:43 AM Updated Oct 28, 2026, 09:43 AM Set as preferred source NEW YORK - The US Federal Election Commission’s website has been targeted by a hacker or hackers, according to an email seen by Reuters, disrupting the agency’s electronic filings system a week before the Nov 3 elections. The cyberattack comes as so-called super political action committees (PACs) and dark money groups spend record sums in the final days of the races. The elections will determine whether US President Donald Trump’s Republicans maintain their majorities in Congress for the next two years. In a statement, the FEC said, “at this time, the FEC’s electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service”. The FEC, which tracks the spending of candidates and political committees, said users could still search the website for past reports. It declined further comment on the outage. The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections and the outage should have no effect on voters’ ability to cast ballots. The outage prevents organisations from filing the FEC’s 24-hour and 48-hour spending reports, which show how much political groups and others are spending on specific races. “I’ve never seen this in 26 years,” said Steven Mele, president and CEO at political finance compliance firm MBA Consulting Group. “The result is there will be less disclosure on the elections” until it is fixed. A status message posted by the FEC said its filing system had been down since around 10pm local time on Oct 26 (10am Singapore time on Oct 27). The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency referred questions to the FEC. The FBI did not immediately return messages seeking comment. The FEC posted the notice after campaign finance officers could not file mandatory reports late on Oct 26. “We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we’ve had to temporarily shut down our web facing services,” an FEC electronic filings officer said in the e-mail to several campaign compliance firms that night. The midterms are now the most expensive US election in history with roughly US$11.21 billion (S$14.4 billion) spent on advertising and future reservations so far, according to political ad tracker AdImpact. It has surpassed the previous record set in the 2024 elections when US$11.2 billion was spent on all races, including US$3.2 billion on the presidential race between Trump and former Vice-President Kamala Harris, AdImpact said. Much of the spending is being driven by super PACs, which can accept unlimited amounts of money from wealthy individuals and corporations and spend as much as they want on campaigns with few restrictions. The sums being spent in recent weeks are staggering as Democrats gain ground in several Republican strongholds. Super PACs and dark money groups have spent an average of over US$50 million per day over the last week, said Brendan Glavin, research director at nonpartisan campaign watchdog group OpenSecrets. More than US$250 million in spending was reported on Oct 20 alone, he added. “It’s a big deal,” he said of the outage, which leaves voters in the dark until the filing system is back online. “These are the key reports that tell us what is happening,” Glavin said. “In the last days of the election this is the only way for us to keep track of where the money’s being spent” and who’s spending it. REUTERS US politics United States Donald Trump US midterm elections

articles.title: SK Hynix $25 Billion Return Cemented by AI Monopoly
articles.content: LivestreamMenuSK Hynix's third-quarter operating profit sharply beat analysts' estimates.Operating profit surged 632.1% from a year ago. In this article South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix on Wednesday posted a record high quarterly profit, sharply beating estimates, and announced over $25 billion in dividends and buybacks, sending shares more than 8% higher. Here are SK Hynix's third-quarter results compared with LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate: Revenue rose 327.9% from a year earlier, while operating profit climbed 632.1% year on year. Compared with the previous quarter, revenue climbed 31.9%, while operating profit surged 37.6%. SK Hynix shares rose more than 8%, outperforming the Kospi's 6.25% gain. The company posted record quarterly revenue and operating profit, with sales exceeding 100 trillion won for the first time, as it announced plans to return about 100 trillion won to shareholders — including at least 30 trillion won in cash dividends and 60 trillion won in share buybacks and cancellations. In the earnings call, SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh-Jung cited financial market volatility and a correction in semiconductor stocks as the main reasons to halt its review of potential pre-IPO fundraising and IPO options for its U.S. subsidiary Solidigm. The company had said it would continue to assess investment timing, scale and financing options to support Solidigm's growth and enhance shareholder value. Kwak also outlined plans to return gains from its investment in Japanese chipmaker Kioxia to shareholders, saying that, "We intend to return the gains realized from our investment in Kioxia this year to our shareholders through a special dividend." The chipmaker approved a third-quarter dividend of 14 trillion won, including a special dividend funded by gains from its investment in Kioxia. SK Hynix will also buyback 20 trillion won in shares, half of which will be cancelled this year, after completing its previously announced 40 trillion won shares buyback last week — which will be cancelled shortly — as mentioned in the earnings call. The company also plans to raise its shareholder return target to more than 50% of cumulative free cash flow generated between 2025 and 2027, as it expects AI investment momentum to continue due to greater adoption of AI services and a more diverse investor base. The company added that it expects the structural supply-demand imbalance in the memory market, where demand outpaces supply, to continue for the time being. SK Hynix expects HBM4 to surpass HBM3E in both shipments and revenue in the fourth quarter, as it ramps up production at its M15X facility in Cheongju, South Korea. HBM, or high-bandwidth memory, is a type of advanced memory used alongside AI processors to handle large amounts of data. HBM4 is the sixth generation of the technology, which started mass productions and shipments in the third quarter. Average selling prices for DRAM rose by a high-20s percentage from the previous quarter, driven by higher conventional DRAM prices and a growing share of higher-priced HBM4 sales. Meanwhile, shipments of server DDR5 memory chips — a type of memory used in data center servers — rose more than 40% from the previous quarter, as said in the call. The company has secured long-term agreements with 14 major customers covering more than 50% of its production capacity for 2027 and 2028, expecting memory demand to outpace supply through 2030 and plans to significantly increase investment next year.

articles.title: Meta Imposes Private Autonomous Governance to Preempt Public AI Regulation
articles.content: Why would anyone trust Meta? After all, this is the company that became the world’s avatar for shameless and exploitative data harvesting. The same data mastery that powers one of the most effective advertising platforms ever made also gave us Cambridge Analytica , whistleblowers like Frances Haugen and Sarah Wynn-Williams , and unflattering films like The Social Dilemma and, just this month, The Social Reckoning . In the Axios -Harris Poll 100 , Meta scored a lowly 59.6, down in the basement with ByteDance and X. Publishers have their own reasons to be suspicious. Meta once vastly increased the reach of its properties, and even paid them for content, then abruptly took it all away when its priorities shifted. Meta has blocked news entirely in Canada since 2023, and briefly did the same in Australia in 2021. So when Nieman Lab reported that Meta had changed its terms of service in a way that seemed to give itself permission to scrape the site of any company with a Meta Business account, nobody was inclined to give it the benefit of the doubt. The new terms, which allow Meta to use automated tools to “access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl” websites “associated with” a business account, and to use that content to “provide, develop, improve, research, train” Meta products, could be interpreted as signing over to Meta the license to do whatever it wants with your content, including training its AI models or even offering up AI answers based on it. Indeed, three legal experts Nieman Lab consulted warned publishers of exactly that danger. . To learn more, visit mediacopilot.substack.com Meta quickly backpedaled, sort of. Within a day, it removed the word train and limited scraped content to its advertising and business products. A spokesperson insisted, “This is not about scraping news sites.” That didn’t calm anyone down. Legal experts said the revised language still permits mass scraping, and publisher groups on both sides of the Atlantic demanded a pause and filed complaints with regulators. This week Meta pushed the effective date from October 30 to November 20. The U.K.’s News Media Association called the delay “ a pause, not a solution .” It’s unlikely that Meta secretly changed its position on what has been, for the past three years, the single most important legal issue in how AI affects media, and then tried to bury it in a terms-of-service update. The impetus for the change was likely more mundane: Meta says the crawling language came from folding its Ad Creative Generative AI Terms into its main commercial terms, and AI tools that build ads for a business presumably need to read that business’s website. As Meta pushes further into agents like its Muse assistant, its bots will need to touch the open web more, not less. But you don’t have to be a conspiracy theorist to see how Meta stepped in it here. The change isn’t irrelevant, and publishers should be concerned about how legal agreements are worded. And some of Meta’s wording is hard to explain away. The terms let Meta create “test credentials,” which Cornell law professor James Grimmelmann said would let it sign up as a fake user to get past registration walls. There’s no opt-out short of abandoning Meta’s business tools. And the change arrived just as Meta began charging some accounts, through its new Meta One subscription, to post links to the same content its bots could crawl for free. And, as I said, Meta has wholly earned its reputation for not considering all the dimensions of how its actions can lead to disastrous consequences . What Meta did here, and the media’s understandable reaction, is a symptom of a deeper problem. Some will blame AI companies’ thirst for data, or a Machiavellian quest to squeeze the media industry, but the real issue is a vacuum of standards and rules around what AI agents, and the crawlers that power them, can and cannot do. You can see this same issue in another freakout from the past week: an Axios report that banks were seeing a growing number of “unauthorized” AI agents accessing customer accounts. While that sounds scary out of context, what it mostly represents is individuals using AI services to access their accounts and take actions on their behalf, not some kind of mass hacking event. Still, there are real concerns around agents the bank didn’t sanction accessing customer accounts, not the least of which is liability when something (inevitably) goes wrong. That’s why JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon told analysts earlier this month that letting in outside agents is “just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan,” and the bank now blocks them from logging in. Schwab is doing the same while steering clients to its own AI assistant (a move that also happens to protect its lucrative cash business), and Citi doesn’t allow third-party agents to log in either. One of the agents getting locked out, incidentally, is Meta’s own Muse. In both cases, the platform saw either an opportunity or a gap with respect to AI usage, and as the party with leverage, it decided the rules. Which is exactly what happens when there are no rules—the person with the biggest gun gets to make them. When it comes to AI, and especially agents, we’re all living in Tombstone. We saw the same dynamic in last year’s dustup between Perplexity and Cloudflare. To recap, Cloudflare accused Perplexity of using stealth crawlers to get around sites’ bot-blocking preferences, and Perplexity insisted its agents were legitimate proxies for actual users, entitled to the same access. Regardless of who you think is right, it’s clear Perplexity had leverage when it was them versus individual sites. But when Cloudflare got involved, the equation changed. As the gatekeeper for a huge share of the web, Cloudflare delisted Perplexity as a verified bot and gave every customer a way to block its stealth crawlers. Perplexity has since deputized itself in another matter, blocking ads that Time served to AI agents as “deceptive” without saying how it defines the term. Certainly, the system would benefit from common rules and standards, and—to stretch the Wild West analogy—we’re beginning to see the townspeople band together. Collective organizations like SPUR (the Standards for Publisher Usage Rights coalition), now more than 80 publishers strong , are looking to establish standards for how publisher content is tracked and valued when AI systems use it. And lawmakers are moving, too: The bipartisan Stealth Bot Prohibition Act in Congress would require crawlers to identify themselves and their purpose. And several states , including New York, have already passed their own versions, so any site that crawlers scrape—not just publishers—will have a better idea of what to do with them. What this means for Meta and anyone else attempting to use their leverage to set the rules: You overreach at your peril. While legal departments will always default to grabbing the widest possible set of rights, that will arouse suspicion and mistrust in a world with no rules to govern those rights, and it’s why it’s not enough for a Meta spokesperson to simply say publishers can still block its crawler with robots.txt. Putting those words in the actual terms of service, as WAN-IFRA, the global publishers’ association, has demanded , would make clear to everyone what rules you think you’re playing under. The fact that those rules are up to Meta at all is the real vacuum. Right now, whoever holds the leverage decides what an agent can do with what it collects: Meta through its terms, JPMorgan through its login page, Perplexity through its index. A three-week delay doesn’t change that. Until someone builds a framework everyone has to follow, you can’t blame publishers for circling the wagons whenever someone pins on a badge and declares themselves the new sheriff in town. . articles.title: French Censorship Orders Force Sovereign DNS Resolver Quad9 Out of Country
articles.content: A nonprofit service that protects internet users’ privacy is leaving France. Quad9, a free DNS resolver, has said it will reluctantly stop serving users in France on November 24. This follows a French court order that Quad9 must block access to websites that are accused of infringing the copyrights of a sports broadcaster. Forcing a responsible privacy service out of an important market is a predictable result of trying to force infrastructure providers to be copyright police. When you visit a website, a DNS resolver reads the domain name you type in—like eff.org — and translates it into a numerical IP address that’s used to direct data across the internet. A DNS resolver can see the names of websites you connect to, so its privacy policies are important. Quad9 is an NGO that’s incorporated in Switzerland, in part to protect its users from data demands. The company also helps protect users from malware and phishing by blocking domains that are known to be malicious. Services like Quad9 offer an alternative to the DNS resolvers of local internet service providers and wireless carriers, which are vulnerable to demands from law enforcement, censorship, and commercial surveillance. In a blog post explaining its decision, Quad9 explains that the French court’s order forces it to make a decision that, either way, is bad for users. It could either “extend French law to the whole world (blocking globally)” or try to identify and block users only in France—something that it can’t do reliably, and a move that could leave the company facing massive fines if it fails to block websites perfectly within France. Quad9 says it is facing about 20 other lawsuits in France seeking similar blocking orders. Rather than accept these demands, Quad9 has decided to withdraw its service from France. That is a real loss for French users who rely on the service to protect their privacy and security. It is also the right thing to do, when faced with the alternative: making promises it can’t keep, or abandoning users’ rights worldwide. Quad9’s decision will not remove any allegedly infringing material from the internet. The organization doesn’t host websites. Users looking for particular websites can easily switch to another DNS resolver. So the material targeted by copyright holders will remain online and accessible, even while they drive a privacy-protecting service out of France. These events matter beyond the borders of France, and U.S. lawmakers should pay attention. Congress is considering multiple site-blocking proposals , which would require ISPs and other intermediaries, including DNS resolvers, to block access to websites in the name of protecting copyright. These bills threaten speech and our ability to access information online, and they are invitations to abuse. The Quad9 withdrawal shows another cost: if internet services get forced into being copyright cops, users can lose services that they rely on for privacy and security. Worse still, if neutral services like Quad9 are forced to build site-blocking systems for the benefit of copyright holders, it becomes far easier for other powerful interests, including repressive governments, to demand the same systems be used to censor speech they dislike, globally. Congress should reject site-blocking bills. They’re a threat to the open internet, and don’t help creators or creativity.

articles.title: Amazon Guts Core Artificial Intelligence Teams After Prolonged Commercial Underperformance
articles.content: Getty Images / Futurism By now, you’d be hard pressed to find anyone who isn’t broadly familiar with the AI heavyweights and their flagship models. OpenAI has ChatGPT, Anthropic has Claude, Google has Gemini. But what does Amazon have? Not a whole lot, it turns out. Unlike its competitors in the tech megacorp scene, Amazon’s standout AI model — organized under the name “Nova” — is about the farthest thing from a household name. And that’s not likely to change anytime soon, because the ecommerce giant is now gutting its in-house AI labs, Bloomberg reports . Per the outlet, Amazon is scaling back the ambitions of most of its Nova AI models and reorganizing its AI development teams as part of an effort to narrow its focus on “highest priority” goals, after its power-hungry large language models turned out to be a bust. Accordingly, the company has put most of its AI models on ice, Amazon insiders told Bloomberg . This includes its text-based Nova models, as well as video- and image-generating models, all of which have been placed in a state of “keep the lights on,” meaning they’re technically still supported, but only receive the bare minimum resources needed to sustain them. Instead, labor and computing power are being diverted toward a singular “frontier-model effort” led by Pieter Abbeel, director of the Berkeley Robot Learning Lab whose robotics company Covariant was hoovered up by Amazon in 2024. At the time Abbeel joined the tech giant, Covariant’s founders were working on AI models for robots, which lines up pretty well with Amazon’s push to automate everything it possibly can. News of the shift in Amazon’s strategic focus comes a week after it closed one of its key AI offices in San Francisco, an 80-person site specializing in research on artificial general intelligence, the supposed next-level of AI development where the tech obtains human-level intelligence and reasoning skills. With urgent questions swirling over whether LLMs can ever usher in a return on investment — let alone AGI — it may be that Amazon is jumping out of the AI hype cycle while it still can. articles.title: Walmart Retrains Two Million Employees to Normalize Generative AI
articles.content: LivestreamMenuAs companies roll out AI tools, many are trying to figure out how employees feel about the technology in their jobs.Walmart recently surveyed its more than 2.1 million associates, and found that those who took advantage of AI training and certification cited higher levels of confidence with the technology.The retailer says associates have access to AI learning and certification programs through OpenAI and Google.In this article As enterprise AI investment continues to grow, companies of all sizes are trying to figure out how employees feel about the technology in the workplace. Walmart, the biggest private employer in the world, asked its 2.1 million associates in June that exact question for the first time, trying to get a sense of how one of the most diverse workforces is experiencing AI. What it found, based on more than 1.7 million survey responses, is that while workers have different levels of familiarity and comfort with AI, training and experience with the technology matters. Seventy-seven percent of Walmart's office-based associates said are excited about AI's potential to improve their work, Walmart Chief People Officer for Associate Experience and Digital Maren Waggoner told CNBC's Leslie Picker at the 2026 CNBC Workforce Executive Council Summit in New York City. And as for Walmart's U.S. frontline associates, 84% said they are confident using digital tools, a reflection of the AI-powered tools that many of them are now using in their roles, she said. "We've given them certificates, we've given them training programs and tools, and so they're using it in their day-to-day," Waggoner said. In the last 13 months, Walmart has partnered with both Google and OpenAI around learning and AI certification programs for associates at no cost. Waggoner said that associates who went through OpenAI training said they had a 27% confidence gain using AI. That has helped Walmart buck some of the larger trends around AI across the country. While about 52% of U.S. adults say they are more concerned than excited about AI, according to an August 2026 Pew Research Center poll, Walmart associates report greater comfort and excitement, Walmart data showed. "Providing the tools, providing the training; they feel more confident," Waggoner said. While AI is perhaps the biggest technological revolution that Walmart has gone through over its 64-year history, Waggoner said the company's approach to transformation has remained the same. "We have a pretty bold mission statement around being a people-led, tech-powered omni-channel retailer that is ultimately dedicated to helping save money," she said. "The people-led and tech-powered piece has been around for a while." Many workers across the economy say they are afraid of AI replacing their jobs. While Waggoner said Walmart is finding ways to use AI to automate processes in fulfillment centers, for example, the retailer's efforts with the technology are to "reduce some of that friction and use robotics to help, and then really focus the work on human judgement." In fact, Waggoner said, at the company's innovation lab in Dallas, Texas, automated efforts to reduce the physical tasks previously performed by humans have instead created more quality assurance-type roles as opposed to broader job losses. And on the front lines of stores, Waggoner said Walmart has found that its customers "actually like talking to a human at checkout." That has allowed associates to focus their efforts on using AI to solve customer challenges. Waggoner pointed to a store manager in Mexico that she met earlier this year who built his own AI agent to look at reports and drive fresh produce sales. "He's using the tool, but he's still running the store," she said. "The store manager job is still there. He's using the tools and technology to drive his business. And by the way, his fresh sales are through the roof."

articles.title: Federal Court Curbs Executive Control Over National Guard Mobilizations
articles.content: Texas National Guard members in Illinois (Brian Cassella/TNS/Newscom)   On October 23, in the case of Newsom v. Trump , the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled Donald Trump's June 2025 federalization of the National Guard in Los Angeles was likely illegal. This decision has little immediate effect, because the National Guard deployment ended months ago, after the Supreme Court ruled against Trump in a related Illinois case . But it has important implications for judicial review of executive invocation of emergency powers to use the military domestically. Among other things, it emphasizes that such actions are reviewable, and the president should get only limited deference. It also adopts a properly restrictive definition of "rebellion" (which is one of the conditions that might justify federalization of the National Guard). Trump federalized the Guard in response to anti-ICE protests. The district court ruled his action was illegal and issued an injunction blocking it. But the Ninth Circuit lifted the preliminary injunction, in a decision I criticized at the time . The relevant statute 10 U.S.C. Section 12406 , can only be used to federalize state forces in one of the following situations: 1) the United States, or any of the Commonwealths or possessions, is invaded or is in danger of invasion by a foreign nation; (2) there is a rebellion or danger of a rebellion against the authority of the Government of the United States; or (3) the President is unable with the regular forces to execute the laws of the United States Last year, the Ninth Circuit ruled ( incorrectly, I think ) that Trump's action might have been permissible under Subsection 3: a situation where "the President is unable with the regular forces to execute the laws of the United States." As the Ninth Circuit acknowledges in their most recent decision, this basis for Trump's actions was undermined by the Supreme Court's December ruling i n the related case of Trump v. Illinois , which held that Subsection 3 can only be invoked when the president is authorized to use regular federal military forces to enforce the law, and those forces are inadequate. These circumstances do not apply to the anti-ICE protests in Los Angeles and Chicago. No one claims that the situation in Los Angeles amounted to an "invasion" by a "foreign nation." Thus, in its most recent decision the Ninth Circuit considered whether Trump's actions were authorized by Subsection 2, which allows federalization of the guard when "there is a rebellion or danger of a rebellion against the authority of the Government of the United States." The majority opinion by Judge Jennifer Sung holds that the determination that there is a "rebellion" is subject to judicial review and can be invalidated " if it "did not reflect a colorable assessment within a range of honest judgment." I think this is overly deferential. For reasons I outlined in an article published last year , there should be little or no deference when the executive invokes extraordinary emergency powers. Still, the Ninth Circuit standard is far from a blank check, and does allow invalidation of executive actions where the claim of rebellion is blatantly wrong - as it was here. Following the district court, the Ninth Circuit defined "rebellion" as "a violent, armed, organized, open and avowed uprising against the government as a whole." This differentiates "rebellion" from smaller-scale violence or other violations of law. I think that definition is largely correct. The court summarizes a wide range of historical evidence supporting it. The Ninth Circuit also concluded that events in Los Angeles did not even come close to meeting that standard. There were some violations of law by protestors, and some small-scale violence. But no systematic effort to overthrow the government or anything close to it. If anything, both this issue and the definition of "rebellion" are easier calls than the court suggests. Judge Sung, author of the majority opinion, is a liberal Biden appointee. But her opinion was joined by Judge Eric Miller, a conservative Trump appointee and onetime clerk for Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas. This suggests the issue here cuts across ideological and jurisprudential lines. Judge Mark Bennett, another Trump appointee, dissented, but mostly on procedural grounds. Judge Bennett did also take issue with the majority's conclusion that if Trump's federalization of the National Guard exceeded his statutory authority, it also violated the Tenth Amendment, which reserves to the states or to "the people," those "powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution." He argues that the power to call forth the National Guard is delegated to Congress by the Calling Forth Clause of the Constitution, which gives Congress power "[t]o provide for calling forth the Militia to execute the Laws of the Union, suppress Insurrections and repel Invasions." This is true enough. But in situations where Congress has not exercised that authority, states retain total control over their militia (of which the National Guard is the principal modern example), and that control is protected by the Tenth Amendment. Indeed, such control over state military forces is a central element of state sovereignty. Overriding it without proper constitutional authority qualifies as unconstitutional "commandeering" of state government forces. As the majority explains: The federal government—whether the President or Congress—violates the Tenth Amendment by commandeering state personnel to enforce or administer federal law. Printz v. United States, 521 U.S. 898, 925 (1997) (Under the Tenth Amendment, "the Federal Government may not compel the States to implement, by legislation or executive action, federal regulatory programs."). If, for example, the President commandeered state police to help federal officers enforce federal immigration laws, that would violate the Tenth Amendment…. California National Guard members are state personnel, unless properly federalized… The President purported to convert the Guard into federal personnel by issuing federalization orders. If those federalization orders had been valid, then the President would have deployed federal officers in Los Angeles, and no commandeering of state personnel would have occurred. But because the President lacked authority to federalize the California National Guard, the federalization orders were invalid, and the deployed Guard members remained state personnel…. In other words, because the deployed members of the California National Guard were not properly federalized, they remained the legal equivalent (for Tenth Amendment purposes) of the state police. And because the challenged executive orders compelled those state officers to help federal officers enforce federal law, the orders violated the Tenth Amendment…. The Tenth Amendment protects States against overreach by the "Federal Government," whether "by legislation or executive action." Printz , 521 U.S. at 925, 935. The President cannot command state officials to enforce federal law even if a federal statute would authorize him, under some other circumstances, to call those officials into federal service. If the statute did not authorize the President to federalize the California Guard members here…, then the federalization orders were invalid, the Guard members remained state personnel, and Defendants violated the Tenth Amendment by commandeering those state personnel to administer federal immigration laws. Exactly so. The majority and dissent consider a number of procedural issues, which I will not try to address. The majority also parses a variety of relevant precedents in detail. I may have more to say about some of them in future writings. For the moment, this decision has little immediate effect. But it sets an important precedent in favor of judicial review of executive invocation of emergency powers, and on the meaning of "rebellion."

articles.title: Finnish Engineering Giant Transforms Marine Manufacturing into Sovereign Energy Backbone
articles.content: Teknologiayhtiö Wärtsilän nousu on osoitus perinteikkään yhtiön kyvystä elää ajassa. Moni mieltää Wärtsilän etenkin laivamoottorien valmistajaksi, ja tuo liiketoiminta on edelleen vakaalla pohjalla. Mutta voimakas kasvu ei suinkaan tule merenkulusta, vaan Wärtsilän voimalaitosbisneksestä. Tekoälystä ja koko maailman sähköistymisestä. – Nykypäivänä meillä on enemmän ihmisiä töissä datan parissa kuin tuotannossa. Tavallisesti ihmiset assosioivat Wärtsilän isoihin moottoreihin, ja ne ovat tärkeitä, mutta digitaaliset ratkaisut ovat vähintäänkin yhtä tärkeitä, sanoo Wärtsilän toimitusjohtaja Håkan Agnevall Ylelle. Agnevallin mukaan jo puolet yhtiön liiketoiminnasta on palveluita. Tekoäly-yhtiöillä on käynnissä valtava kilpajuoksu siitä, kuka saa datakeskuksensa pystyyn nopeimmin. Massiivisten hankkeiden suurimpia pullonkauloja on niiden valtava energiantarve, ja varsinkin Yhdysvalloissa ongelmaa on ratkottu Wärtsilän voimalaitoksilla. Ei tarvitse odottaa sähkölinjojen valmistumista, kun takapihalla pörräävät suomalaiset moottorit. ”Vihreä ei ole mustavalkoinen asia”, sanoo Wärtsilän puikkoihin vuonna 2021 tullut ruotsalainen Håkan Agnevall. Sillä hän tarkoittaa, että moottorivoimalat ovat kelpo välivaiheen tuote, kun siirrytään kohti päästötöntä sähköntuotantoa. Samaan aikaan maailmanlaajuinen sähköistyminen etenee nopeammin kuin on odotettu, mikä tarkoittaa lisää tarvetta vakaalle säätövoimalle, joka paikkaa tuuli- ja aurinkovoiman epävakautta. Wärtsilälle se näkyy jo isoina tilauksina rapakkojen taakse: Australiaan lähtee 13 kaasumoottoria ja Yhdysvaltoihin 15. Yhtiö on siis ollut oikeassa paikassa oikeaan aikaan, ja kenties vielä oikeasta maasta. Kiristynyt geopolitiikka saa niin yrityksiä kuin valtioita miettimään yhä tarkemmin, missä päin maailmaa kauppaa käydään ja kenen kanssa. Hyvä maine ja vakaa valtio ovat kullanarvoista valuuttaa, ja menestystä edesauttaa myös Suomen ja Yhdysvaltojen diili jäänmurtajista. Niihinkin laivoihin päätyy Wärtsilän teknologiaa. Myös Suomen hallitus valmistelee paraikaa energiatuotannon investointitukea, joka voi sataa Wärtsilän laariin. Ilmasto- ja ympäristöministeri Sari Multala sanoi Iltalehdelle syyskuussa, että tuen kohteina voisivat olla esimerkiksi nopeasti käynnistettävät, biokaasulla toimivat turbiinit. Avaa kuvien katselu OP:n analyytikko Jussi Mikkonen seuraa Wärtsilää. Kuva: Berislav Jurišić / Yle Wärtsilä julkaisi tiistaina tuoreen osavuosikatsauksensa. Tulos on vahva, sanoo Wärtsilää seuraava OP:n analyytikko Jussi Mikkonen Ylelle. – Wärtsilä saa paljon moottoritilauksia. Meidän arviomme on, että hyvä kysyntä tulee jatkumaan vielä ainakin pari vuotta. Edellisvuoden heinä-syyskuuhun verrattuna Wärtsilän liikevaihto kasvoi 7 prosenttia ja vertailukelpoinen liiketulos 19 prosenttia. Yhtiön ydintoiminnoissa eli merenkulussa ja energiassa tilauskertymä kasvoi 47 prosentia. Lisää: Wärtsilän vuosi jatkuu edelleen kovassa vauhdissa Ohita infografiikka Koko Suomen konepajateollisuuteen verrattuna Mikkonen pitää Wärtsilän nousua poikkeuksellisena. Yhtiön ongelmat ovat oikeastaan postiivisia, koska kysyntää olisi enemmänkin kuin Wärtsilällä on tarjontaa. – Energian vahvan tilauskertymän vuoksi moottoreidemme toimitusajat pitenevät edelleen, osavuosikatsauksessa kerrotaan. Wärtsilä on kuluvan vuoden aikana kertonut jo kahteen otteeseen lisäävänsä tuotantokapasiteettiaan. Laajennusten myötä vuonna 2029 yhtiön tuotantokapasiteetti kasvaa 65 prosenttia . Ihan kaikki Wärtsilällä ei ole mennyt putkeen. OP:n Mikkosen mukaan energiavarastoinnilla pyyhkii heikommin. Siksi Wärtsilä erotti sen osan itsestään lokakuun alussa yhteisyritykseksi, josta saksalainen RCT Solutions omistaa nykyisin puolet. Agnevallin mukaan energiavarastoinnin haasteiden taustalla ovat lisääntynyt kilpailu ja Yhdysvaltain tuontitullit, jotka nostavat Wärtsilän akkujen hintaa Atlantin toisella puolella. Vaikka Wärtsilä yllätti sijoittajat kirjaamalla enemmän tilauksia kuin analyytikot olivat ennakoineet, ei yhtiön osakekurssi muuttanut linjaansa, vaan jyrkensi pidempään jatkunutta alamäkeään. Osakkeen hinta romahti noin 8 prosenttia tiistaina. Ohita infografiikka Sijoittajat saattoivat reagoida Wärtsilän varovaisiin taloustavoitteisiin, OP:n Mikkonen arvioi Reutersille . Uusissa tavoitteissa Wärtsilä tähtää matalaan kaksinumeroiseen prosentuaaliseen kasvuun liikevaihdossa ja 16 prosentin kasvuun liiketuloksessa. Sijoittajat odottivat datakeskusbuumin keskellä vieläkin kovempia tavoitteita. – Pörssiyhtiön johtajana olen oppinut keskittymään asiakkaisiin ja toimittamaan tuloksia. Antaa osakemarkkinoiden tehdä omat taikansa, Agnevall sanoo Ylelle.

articles.content: LivestreamMenuAnthropic had $112.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents and $19.3 billion in short-term investments as of June 30.The $131.7 billion total exceeded every non-bank U.S. company in CNBC and S&P Capital IQ data except Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet.Never before has a company gone public with anywhere near this amount of cash.watch nowVIDEO09:08Anthropic's cash rules tech peers: Here's what to knowSquawk BoxAnthropic has more cash than almost every company in America. The nearly 6-year-old artificial intelligence lab disclosed on Monday in an S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission that it had $112.4 billion in cash, plus another $19.3 billion in short-term investments, as of June 30. Anthropic's total of $131.7 billion surpasses every non-bank U.S. company, except for Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet, according to data compiled by CNBC and S&P Capital IQ. As of midyear, Anthropic had more cash than Amazon, SpaceX, Meta and Microsoft. It had more than Nvidia and Apple combined. Depending on how much the company raises in its initial public offering — and reports suggest it could top $100 billion — Anthropic could bump its hoard to more than $230 billion in cash. So far, Anthropic hasn't shared specific details about its offering size, and it said in the filing that existing investors would also be selling into the IPO – meaning the company itself won't collect the entire fundraise. Those details are expected to be disclosed in about two weeks. Never before has a company gone public with anywhere near this amount of cash. Anthropic's trove underscores the fundraising prowess that has allowed it to amass an aggregate of $141 billion in private financing in just six years since its founding. However, given the company's future commitments for computing power that have yet to hit its expenses, Anthropic will have to continue accumulating cash through fundraising or generating profits to fulfill its obligations. Anthropic's first-half compute and infrastructure expenses totaled $8.95 billion. But the company said it usually buys computing power 12 to 18 months ahead of time, and only recognizes expenses as that capacity becomes available. That means the first-half expense figure doesn't capture the full scale of its future obligations. As of June 30, Anthropic disclosed $321.4 billion in estimated future undiscounted lease obligations and $265.6 billion in expected future fixed or minimum-guaranteed commitments — more than half a trillion total. These will commence within the next few years, with terms ranging from one year to 20 years. Additionally, the company said that subsequent to June 30, it entered into new and amended agreements with a minimum future payment obligation of about $245 billion. The company hasn't shared an aggregate amount of its up-to-date commitments yet. If Anthropic's cash is king, compute is its biggest claim on the crown. —CNBC's Ritika Shah and Nick Wells contributed to this article.

articles.title: OpenAI Cracks Down on Automated Hallucinated Bug Reports
articles.content: Even OpenAI is admitting there is a lot of AI slop in the security space.  An executive for the frontier AI company said Tuesday that AI -generated vulnerability reports are overwhelming open-source maintainers, leading some to stop accepting submissions as the workload exceeds their capacity to review them. Michael Aiello, OpenAI’s cyber executive in residence, described the problem during a question-and-answer session Tuesday at the DataTribe Challenge in Washington, D.C., when he was asked how he viewed OpenAI ’s Patch the Planet program versus open-source maintainers banning AI-based submissions because of concerns about quality and clarity.  “It’s an ecosystem problem where that [maintainer] is just not going to respond to hundreds and hundreds of AI-submitted vulnerabilities,” Aiello said.  He contrasted the volume against his company’s own program, which partners with security research organizations to identify vulnerabilities, develop fixes and help bring them into the affected projects. According to the company’s website , 661 patches have been developed and tested, with 458 of them accepted by maintainers for inclusion in the projects they oversee.  However, Aiello said those involved with Daybreak often coordinate with maintainers, as opposed to just sending a message into GitHub and hoping for the best.  He further described the broader burden on maintainers, who are often tasked with running through hundreds of AI-generated reports to determine validity, the security implications and evaluate the proposed fix. “In most cases, they’re likely real bugs of some degree,” he said. “It’s, ‘Are they critical bugs?’ And are they bugs worth the time of the maintainers?…The result is they’ve just stopped taking” submissions. Aiello further laid out advice for those that do create vulnerability disclosures for open-source maintainers, including more work in establishing the quality of the finding, writing an understandable report and allocating resources to coordinate disclosure once a report is filed. “Make sure they’re really high quality, make sure it’s consumable and readable by a single person, and then spend your own resources coordinating vulnerability disclosure,” he said. “You need to now coordinate the vulnerability disclosure across the whole ecosystem, which is itself another project.” Aiello used OpenAI’s work on the recent PHP vulnerabilities as an example of that coordination. He said a partner research organization discovered the flaw, and OpenAI worked with the PHP Foundation to validate it, develop a fix and coordinate its release. “You have to work with response partners, and you have to work with the operators to actually issue the patch,” he said. The process involved coordinating with a broad group of organizations, extending the work from technical review through patch release. Aiello acknowledged difficulties in carrying out the entire process. “Now, did it go perfectly? No,” he said. “We’re learning as we do this over time.”

Under Article 27 of the act, posting advertisements without approval carries a fine of N$1,200 to NT$100,000, the department said. People should not trust unfamiliar QR code links posted on public signs, as criminals could exploit them to steal money or personal information, police said. People should verify links with government agencies or call 110 for assistance, they said. Parking meters are public facilities and not places for private advertising, the transportation department said, adding that it would step up enforcement in collaboration with police and the Taipei Department of Environmental Protection. The only platforms offering self-service roadside parking payment options are the Parking Loudspeaker (停車大聲公) and Space4Car (易停網) apps, the transportation department said. articles.title: Automated Enterprise Orchestration Bridges Fragmented African Cloud Infrastructure Deficits
articles.content: Business Wire via ITWeb, CUPERTINO, Calif.-, 27 Oct 2026 Unframe , the Applied AI Lab, announced its availability on all three leading cloud marketplaces: AWS Marketplace , Google Cloud Marketplace and Microsoft Marketplace . For enterprises, cloud marketplaces have become the preferred channel for discovering and procuring software. AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft together serve the vast majority of enterprise cloud infrastructure worldwide. Their marketplaces represent a growing share of how organizations purchase technology by consolidating vendor relationships, simplifying contracting and allowing companies to apply existing cloud spend toward new solutions. Being listed across all three is now a key expectation for enterprise-grade software vendors. “Enterprises shouldn’t have to choose between moving quickly on AI and working within the procurement and cloud frameworks they already have,” said Jacquelyn Goldberg , Global VP of Revenue at Unframe. “As an applied AI lab, our job is to close the gap between what AI can do and what enterprises actually run in production. Making Unframe available across AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft marketplaces removes another barrier between identifying a high-value use case and putting it into production.” Enterprises can purchase Unframe directly through AWS Marketplace , Google Cloud Marketplace and Microsoft Marketplace . Each listing allows procurement teams to transact through their existing cloud accounts, applying committed cloud spend toward Unframe and working within established approval workflows. Private offers are available on all three platforms, enabling Unframe to structure tailored commercial agreements — including pricing, contract terms and usage parameters — delivered directly through a customer's cloud account. For enterprises already invested in one of these platforms, purchasing Unframe through the marketplace streamlines procurement and accelerates the path to AI outcomes. Unframe delivers tailored, production-ready AI solutions in days with measurable business impact in weeks. Marketplace availability extends that principle to procurement itself. Instead of navigating separate vendor contracts, legal reviews and procurement cycles, customers can transact within an ecosystem they already trust and use. In addition to simplifying the procurement process, the marketplace enables organizations to draw down on existing cloud and AI commitments, eliminating the need for new budget allocations. Choosing Unframe doesn’t mean introducing another foundational AI platform. Unframe sits on top of and complements the cloud, model, data and AI platforms enterprises have already invested in, including AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. We provide the enterprise application, orchestration and governance layer that turns those foundational capabilities into production-ready use cases. This helps customers get more value from their existing cloud investments, drives greater adoption and consumption of the underlying hyperscaler platforms and preserves flexibility across models and infrastructure. Enterprises can connect with the Unframe team at contact@unframe.ai or schedule a call. Share About Unframe Unframe is the Applied AI Lab dedicated to closing the gap between AI capabilities and AI adoption within enterprises. We meet organizations where they are: end-to-end managed delivery, dedicated expertise for teams that self-build or strategic advisory. All on a proven platform built for speed, governance and enterprise scale. Unframe solutions run in the customer's preferred environment, integrating with existing AI programs and core systems. Unframe is headquartered in Cupertino, California, with a global presence in Tel Aviv and Berlin.
